chunks.title: Alex Hormozi (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Main teachings
chunks.text:
- Value Equation: perceived value goes up with the dream outcome and the perceived likelihood of achieving it, and goes down with time delay and effort and sacrifice. To raise value, fix the weakest of the four.
- Grand Slam Offer: stack bonuses, guarantees and scarcity so the offer is clearly worth more than the price, so you compete on value, not price.
- Risk reversal: guarantees lower the buyer's fear.
- Naming: make the offer name speak to a specific person, result and timeframe.
- Fund growth with customer cash flow; favor recurring and referral revenue.

chunks.title: Alex Hormozi (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Failures and mistakes
chunks.text: He went broke twice early on, including after a partnership collapsed. Payment processors held his revenue for months because his business was flagged high-risk. After selling Gym Launch he said he felt poorer because the cash-flow engine was gone. He has publicly broken down his own content mistakes.

chunks.title: Alex Hormozi (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Evidence check
chunks.text: His frameworks are expert opinion from his own industries (gyms, info products), not tested in controlled studies. The value equation lines up with well-known ideas in pricing and consumer psychology, but numbers like "10x value" are rules of thumb.

chunks.title: Alex Hormozi (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Criticisms
chunks.text: Critics say the books simplify things, may not transfer to every industry, pay little attention to ethics and sustainability, and his free content funnels into expensive programs.

chunks.title: Alex Hormozi (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Practical application (videography business)
chunks.text:
- Write one clear offer per niche: for example "a 60-second cinematic wedding highlight delivered in 14 days, or the edit is free".
- Raise perceived likelihood with proof: 3-5 sample films, testimonials, a clear process.
- Cut perceived effort: a simple booking link, a shot list template, one call to plan.
- Use referrals and recurring retainers (monthly content for gyms, restaurants, real estate agents) to smooth income.

chunks.title: Alex Hormozi (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Sources are secondary profiles and a study guide, not the books themselves; quoted figures (sale price, portfolio revenue) are as reported. Reading his books directly is a remaining gap.

chunks.title: Negotiation: first offers as anchors
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In negotiation, the first number on the table tends to pull the final deal toward it. Galinsky and Mussweiler found that whoever made the first offer usually got the better outcome, and that the anchor's pull could be weakened when the other side focused on the first mover's alternatives or on their own target.

chunks.title: Negotiation: first offers as anchors
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Quote first when you know the market: name a confident, well-justified package price (for example a premium wedding package), then explain the value.
- When a client anchors low, do not argue the number. Shift focus to the outcome and your package options, and restate your own target.
- Prepare your walk-away price and your best alternative before any call.

chunks.title: Negotiation: first offers as anchors
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Lab negotiations with students; real deals involve relationships and repeat business.

chunks.title: Setting goals that actually drive performance
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Specific, difficult goals lead to better performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. The effect is strongest when the person is committed, gets feedback on progress, and has the ability and strategy for the task.

chunks.title: Setting goals that actually drive performance
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Make goals specific and measurable: "+15 lb lean by late February", "$10K/month from videography".
- Add feedback: weekly weigh-in average, monthly revenue check.
- For complex goals (building a business), set learning goals first ("test 3 offers this month") before outcome goals.

chunks.title: Setting goals that actually drive performance
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Very difficult goals without the skills to reach them can lead to shortcuts or burnout.

chunks.title: How long habits take to form
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Habits do not form in 21 days. In a 12-week study of 96 people who picked a daily eating, drinking or exercise behavior, it took a median of 66 days for the behavior to become close to automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days. Missing a single day did not meaningfully set people back.

chunks.title: How long habits take to form
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Automaticity rises quickly at first, then levels off.
- Simpler behaviors (drinking water) became automatic faster than harder ones (exercise).
- Same cue, same time, same place each day helped.

chunks.title: How long habits take to form
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Expect about 2-3 months of conscious effort before a new routine feels automatic. Plan for it.
- Anchor the habit to a fixed cue: "after I brush my teeth in the morning, I read one chapter".
- Never miss twice: one missed day does not break a habit, two starts a new pattern.
- Start smaller than you think, then grow it once it is automatic.

chunks.title: How long habits take to form
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Small, self-reported study; many participants dropped data. The median hides huge individual variation.

chunks.title: If-then plans (implementation intentions)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Turning a goal into a specific "if situation X, then I will do Y" plan makes people much more likely to follow through. A meta-analysis of 94 studies (over 8,000 people) found a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65) on goal attainment.

chunks.title: If-then plans (implementation intentions)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Write if-then plans for the moments you usually fail: "If it's 5:30 pm on a weekday, then I drive straight to the gym in my gym clothes."
- Plan for obstacles: "If I'm tempted to skip the meal prep Sunday, then I start with just cooking the rice."
- Make the "when" and "where" exact. Vague intentions are what fail.

chunks.title: If-then plans (implementation intentions)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Effects are smaller for very complex goals and when the underlying goal is weak.

chunks.title: Why we procrastinate and how to beat it
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Procrastination is mostly about motivation over time, not laziness. Steel's meta-analysis found the strongest predictors were how unpleasant the task feels, how far away the reward is, low confidence you can do it, and impulsiveness and distractibility.

chunks.title: Why we procrastinate and how to beat it
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Shrink the task until it is not aversive: "edit the first 30 seconds of the wedding film", not "edit the film".
- Bring the reward closer: set a near deadline, tell the client a date, reward yourself right after.
- Build confidence with quick wins first.
- Remove distractions during work blocks (phone in another room, one tab).

chunks.title: Why we procrastinate and how to beat it
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Mostly correlational data from students and self-reports.

chunks.title: Is willpower a limited tank? (ego depletion)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The popular idea that willpower is a fuel tank that runs out with use is disputed. A preregistered replication across 23 labs and over 2,000 participants found an effect close to zero. Self-control is better built by designing your environment and routines than by trying to "save" willpower.

chunks.title: Is willpower a limited tank? (ego depletion)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Remove decisions: lay out gym clothes, prep meals, keep junk food out of the house, phone outside the bedroom.
- Make the good choice the easy default and the bad choice inconvenient.
- Do not tell yourself you "used up" willpower; that belief itself may make you quit sooner.

chunks.title: Is willpower a limited tank? (ego depletion)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: The debate continues; some researchers argue the replication task was too weak. Treat "willpower tank" claims as unsupported, not as proven false.

chunks.title: What the Bible says about discipline and self-control
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Scripture treats discipline as part of following Christ, not as self-improvement for its own sake. Paul uses the athlete as a picture of the Christian life: training with purpose and self-control for a prize that lasts. Self-control is listed as a fruit of the Spirit, which means it grows from life with God, not from willpower alone.

chunks.title: What the Bible says about discipline and self-control
chunks.heading: Scripture (text)
chunks.text:
- 1 Corinthians 9:24-25 (WEB): "Don't you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win. Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible."
- 1 Corinthians 9:26-27 (WEB): "I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air, but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected."
- Hebrews 12:11 (WEB) begins: "All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous;" and goes on to say that afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
- Galatians 5:22-23 lists self-control among the fruit of the Spirit (read the passage at the link).
- Proverbs 25:28 compares a person without self-control to a city whose walls are broken down (read at the link).
- 2 Timothy 1:7 says God gave a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control (read at the link; some translations say "sound mind" or "discipline").

chunks.title: What the Bible says about discipline and self-control
chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
- 1 Corinthians 9: Paul explains why he gives up his rights for the sake of the gospel. The athlete image is about purposeful self-denial for others and for an eternal prize, not about body image. Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, so readers knew athletes' training well.
- Hebrews 12: "discipline" there is God's fatherly training through hardship; it is the backdrop for enduring difficulty with hope.
- Galatians 5: self-control is the Spirit's fruit set against "the works of the flesh"; the contrast is about walking by the Spirit.

chunks.title: What the Bible says about discipline and self-control
chunks.heading: Interpretation (labeled)
chunks.text: Across Christian traditions, these passages are read as calling believers to train habits (prayer, Scripture, work, the body) with eternal purpose, depending on God's grace rather than pride. Denominations differ on emphasis (for example, the role of spiritual disciplines vs grace), not on self-control being good.

chunks.title: What the Bible says about discipline and self-control
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Tie physical training to purpose: stewardship of the body and energy to serve others.
- Pair the gym habit with a small spiritual habit at the same time each day (for example reading one chapter before the first meal).
- When motivation is low, pray for self-control as fruit to grow, and keep the habit small rather than skipping it.

chunks.title: What the Bible says about discipline and self-control
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Exact quotes are from the public-domain World English Bible; other translations word verses differently. Historical notes on Corinth are standard background, not yet linked to a specific scholarly source here.

chunks.title: Alcohol and muscle building
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Heavy drinking after training reduces muscle building. In a controlled study, a large amount of alcohol after exercise lowered muscle protein synthesis even when protein was eaten with it, though protein reduced the damage.

chunks.title: Alcohol and muscle building
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Avoid heavy drinking on training days, especially after leg or upper sessions you care about.
- If drinking, keep it moderate, eat protein, hydrate, and do not let it cut sleep.
- Alcohol also adds empty calories and often causes next-day facial puffiness.

chunks.title: Alcohol and muscle building
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: One acute study of a large dose in a small group of men; light drinking was not tested.

chunks.title: Daily steps and long-term health
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: More daily steps were linked to lower risk of death, with benefits leveling off around 8,000-10,000 steps a day for adults under 60 and 6,000-8,000 for older adults.

chunks.title: Daily steps and long-term health
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- 8,000-10,000 steps covers most of the health benefit. Higher counts are fine but burn more calories, which must be eaten back on a bulk.
- Walking is a low-fatigue way to stay fit without hurting recovery.

chunks.title: Daily steps and long-term health
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Observational data: association, not proof of cause.

chunks.title: IGF-1 LR3 and unapproved peptides (status and risks)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: IGF-1 LR3 is a modified (long-acting) form of insulin-like growth factor 1. It is not an FDA-approved drug and is sold as a "research chemical". It is banned in sport: the 2026 WADA Prohibited List names IGF-1 and its analogues, including LR3-IGF-1, under S2.3 growth factors. Claims that it builds muscle in healthy people come from anecdotes, not controlled human trials.

chunks.title: IGF-1 LR3 and unapproved peptides (status and risks)
chunks.heading: Key facts
chunks.text:
- Regulators flagged many compounded peptides over safety concerns (immune reactions, impurities, hard-to-characterize ingredients, too little human safety data). In 2023 the FDA placed a group of peptides in its "Category 2" (significant safety risks) list for compounding; in April 2026 it moved several peptides out of Category 2 pending an advisory committee review, which does not mean they are approved.
- Products sold online are not quality-controlled; contents and sterility are unknown.
- IGF-1 activity affects blood sugar; low blood sugar is a known risk of IGF-1 drugs.

chunks.title: IGF-1 LR3 and unapproved peptides (status and risks)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- The app never gives doses, schedules, combinations or ways to use these products.
- If he uses or considers them: do it only under a qualified doctor's supervision, with bloodwork (including glucose) and an honest discussion of risks; stop and seek care for symptoms like shakiness, sweating, confusion or chest pain.
- The proven levers for muscle (hard progressive training, enough protein and calories, sleep, creatine) carry far more evidence.

chunks.title: IGF-1 LR3 and unapproved peptides (status and risks)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Regulatory status changes; re-check by the review date. This is safety and status information, not medical advice.

chunks.title: How much sleep adults need
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Adults should regularly sleep 7 or more hours a night for health. Sleeping less on a regular basis is linked with weight gain, worse mood and performance, impaired immunity and higher risk of several diseases. More than 9 hours may be appropriate for young adults, after sleep debt, or during illness.

chunks.title: How much sleep adults need
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Treat 8 hours in bed as the training target, to get 7+ hours of actual sleep.
- Keep a consistent wake time, even on weekends; it anchors the body clock.
- Morning light, no caffeine within about 8 hours of bed, a cool dark room, and phones out of bed.

chunks.title: How much sleep adults need
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Consensus based on reviewing the evidence, mostly observational links rather than trials of sleep extension.

chunks.title: Caffeine and pre-workout
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Caffeine reliably improves many types of performance, including strength and endurance. The ISSN reports benefits at about 3-6 mg per kg taken about an hour before, with lower amounts also helping some people. The cost is sleep: in a controlled study, a large dose (400 mg) even 6 hours before bed cut sleep by more than an hour.

chunks.title: Caffeine and pre-workout
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Use the smallest amount that works and keep it at least 8 hours before bed for evening sleepers.
- Count all sources: coffee, pre-workout, energy drinks.
- If training in the evening, consider caffeine-free sessions to protect sleep, which matters more for growth.

chunks.title: Caffeine and pre-workout
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Response varies with genetics and habitual intake. People with heart conditions, anxiety or high blood pressure should check with a doctor.

chunks.title: Cutting and contest prep for natural lifters
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: When cutting, slow fat loss and high protein protect muscle. The review recommends losing about 0.5-1% of body weight per week, protein of about 2.3-3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass, fat at about 15-30% of calories, and carbs filling the rest to support training.

chunks.title: Cutting and contest prep for natural lifters
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Cut only when the bulk has added enough fat to justify it; at under 10% body fat, a lean bulk is usually the better use of time.
- Never use dehydration, diuretics or extreme deficits. They cost muscle and can be dangerous.
- Keep lifting heavy and hard during a cut; it is the signal to keep muscle.

chunks.title: Cutting and contest prep for natural lifters
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Much bodybuilding-specific data are case studies; recommendations are a synthesis, not tested as a full protocol.

chunks.title: Creatine monohydrate
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Creatine monohydrate is the most researched sports supplement. The ISSN position stand concludes it improves high-intensity exercise capacity and lean mass gains from training, and is safe for healthy people at the intakes studied (commonly 3-5 g per day, sometimes after a short loading phase).

chunks.title: Creatine monohydrate
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Monohydrate is the form with the evidence; other forms are not shown to be better.
- Daily consistency matters more than timing.
- Expect 1-2 lb of early weight gain, mostly water inside muscle; that is not fat.
- Anyone with kidney disease or on medications should check with a doctor first.

chunks.title: Creatine monohydrate
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Position stands are written by experts in the field. Claims of hair loss come from one small study measuring DHT, not hair loss itself; it has not been replicated.

chunks.title: Lean bulking: surplus size and rate of gain
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A trained lifter can only build muscle so fast, so a big surplus mostly adds fat. Reviews suggest a modest surplus and a slow gain of about 0.25-0.5% of body weight per week. In elite athletes, a guided surplus added more lean mass than eating freely, but also more fat.

chunks.title: Lean bulking: surplus size and rate of gain
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- At about 175 lb: aim for roughly 0.4-0.9 lb per week on the 7-day average.
- Adjust calories by about 100-200 kcal only after 2-3 weeks of trend data.
- Track waist weekly: if the waist climbs fast while strength stalls, the surplus is too big.
- Keep protein about 1.6-2.2 g/kg and fill the rest with carbs to fuel training.

chunks.title: Lean bulking: surplus size and rate of gain
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: The off-season review is narrative and the trial was in elite athletes over 8-12 weeks. Individual gain rates vary widely.

chunks.title: Protein per meal and meal timing
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The body uses protein from large meals too; the old "30 g per meal" limit is a myth for total use, though muscle building per meal may plateau. A practical target is about 0.4 g/kg per meal across at least four meals (up to about 0.55 g/kg per meal for the high end of daily needs).

chunks.title: Protein per meal and meal timing
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Spread protein over 4-5 meals of roughly 30-45 g for a 79 kg lifter, including breakfast and a meal within a few hours around training.
- Exact post-workout timing matters little if daily protein is high and meals are spread out.
- A pre-bed protein meal (for example Greek yogurt) is a reasonable way to add one more feeding.

chunks.title: Protein per meal and meal timing
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Recommendations are extrapolated from acute muscle protein synthesis studies, not long-term growth trials.

chunks.title: How much protein to build muscle
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Eating more protein helps muscle gain from lifting up to about 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day on average, with the upper confidence limit near 2.2 g/kg. Above that, there was no further measurable benefit for most people.

chunks.title: How much protein to build muscle
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Protein supplementation increased gains in fat-free mass and strength from training.
- The benefit plateaued around 1.62 g/kg/day (95% CI up to about 2.2 g/kg/day).
- The effect is larger in trained lifters than beginners, and smaller with age.

chunks.title: How much protein to build muscle
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- At 79 kg (175 lb): about 127 g/day covers most people; 175 g/day covers the high end. A 200 g target is safe for a healthy person but not required; extra calories may be better spent on carbs for training.
- Total daily protein matters most; food or shakes both count.

chunks.title: How much protein to build muscle
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Most included trials were 6-24 weeks. Needs during a cut (calorie deficit) are higher; see the contest-prep review.

chunks.title: Brad Schoenfeld (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Brad Schoenfeld is one of the most published researchers on muscle hypertrophy. His reviews and meta-analyses on volume, frequency, load, rest and protein timing shape much of today's evidence-based bodybuilding advice.

chunks.title: Brad Schoenfeld (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Main teachings
chunks.text:
- Mechanical tension is the main driver of growth.
- Volume has a dose-response relationship with growth; about 10+ hard sets per muscle per week is a good baseline.
- With equal weekly volume, frequency matters little; training each muscle twice a week is a practical default.
- A wide range of loads builds muscle if sets are hard; heavy loads build more strength.
- Longer rests (2-3 minutes) help keep set quality high.

chunks.title: Brad Schoenfeld (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Evidence check
chunks.text: His positions come from meta-analyses of controlled trials, the strongest evidence available in this field. Their limits: short studies, young subjects, and site-specific muscle measures.

chunks.title: Brad Schoenfeld (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Where experts disagree
chunks.text: Researchers still debate how high volume should go before returns flatten, and how much stretch-position training adds.

chunks.title: Brad Schoenfeld (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text: Use his findings as the default rules for programming, then adjust to personal recovery, schedule and lagging muscles.

chunks.title: Brad Schoenfeld (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: This profile covers his research positions, not biography details; those are not yet researched in this library.

chunks.title: Eric Helms (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Eric Helms is a researcher and coach focused on natural (drug-free) bodybuilding and strength sport. His reviews translate research into practical guidelines for bulking (off-season) and cutting (contest prep).

chunks.title: Eric Helms (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Main teachings
chunks.text:
- Natural lifters should gain and lose slowly: slow off-season gains limit fat, slow cuts protect muscle.
- High protein during a cut (relative to fat-free mass) helps keep muscle.
- Effort (reps in reserve) and progressive overload matter more than exotic techniques.
- Supplements are minor; creatine and caffeine are among the few with good support.

chunks.title: Eric Helms (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Evidence check
chunks.text: His guidance is based on systematic reading of the evidence, but much of the bodybuilding-specific data are case studies and small samples; he flags these limits himself.

chunks.title: Eric Helms (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text: For a lean bulk: modest surplus, weekly average weight trend, protein about 1.6-2.2 g/kg, hard progressive training, and patience across months.

chunks.title: Eric Helms (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Profile based on two of his reviews; his books and later work are not yet researched in this library.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Greg Plitt (1977-2015) was a fitness model, trainer and motivational speaker from Maryland. He graduated from West Point (class of 2000), was Airborne and Ranger qualified and served five years as an Army Ranger. He then became one of the most-photographed fitness cover models (Muscle & Fitness, Men's Health, Men's Fitness and others), starred in Bravo's Work Out, and built a large following through intense motivational videos. He died on January 17, 2015, at 37, when he was struck by a train in Burbank, California, while filming a video.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Expertise and achievements
chunks.text:
- Military leadership and physical training background (West Point, Rangers).
- Created the MFT28 ("Military Fitness Trainer") 28-day program published on Bodybuilding.com, plus stair challenges like "1044 Steps to Paradise".
- MET-Rx athlete team member; their 2012 Athlete of the Year.
- His physique was used as a body reference for Dr. Manhattan in Watchmen (2009).

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Philosophy and teachings
chunks.text:
- Training is a vehicle for character: every rep should mean something beyond looks.
- Do the hard things most people avoid; the difficult tasks are the least done and the most rewarding.
- Stay the course and keep focus; success compounds from consistent effort.
- Live so you can look back without regret, and ask how you want to be remembered.
- Take calculated risks rather than being ruled by fear.
- Build a personal brand by being genuinely yourself and using your personality to lift others.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Proven strategies (what holds up)
chunks.text:
- High-effort sessions, consistency and accountability: these line up with the research on proximity to failure and habit formation.
- Military-style structure (set times, set routines) is a sound way to remove daily decision-making.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Failures and mistakes
chunks.text: - His death came from filming near an active train line. Reported accounts say he may have tried to outrun the train; this is reported, not confirmed. The lesson that applies: intensity is not the same as taking unnecessary physical risks.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Evidence check
chunks.text:
- His methods were coaching experience, not tested programs. Many of his workouts were very high volume and high intensity; that works for some, but research shows growth comes from enough hard sets, progression and recovery, not maximal punishment.
- No published data show MFT28 outcomes. Treat it as one structured program among many.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Where his advice may be outdated
chunks.text: - Some period fitness media favored extreme cuts for shoots. For a lean bulk, slow gain and sleep matter more than photo-shoot leanness.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Use his mindset as fuel for consistency and standards (show up, finish the set, do the hard thing first), and use evidence-based programming for the actual sets, reps and food.
- Pair motivation with systems: a scheduled session, a logged workout and a measured weekly result.

chunks.title: Greg Plitt (expert profile)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Biographical facts come from an encyclopedia with citations and a publisher tribute; his teachings are paraphrased from those sources, not from a full review of his video archive. More profile research on his videos and nutrition views is still a gap.

chunks.title: Cardio while building muscle (interference effect)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Moderate cardio does not stop you from building muscle, but a lot of it, especially running, can blunt gains in size and strength. The interference grew with more frequent and longer cardio sessions; cycling interfered less than running.

chunks.title: Cardio while building muscle (interference effect)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- On a bulk, keep hard cardio to about 2-3 sessions a week of 20-30 minutes; walking (like his step goal) has little interference.
- Separate hard cardio from leg training by several hours, or do it on another day.
- Eat back what cardio burns: 15,000 steps a day can add several hundred calories of expenditure.
- Keep some conditioning for heart health and work capacity; the goal is managing dose, not avoiding cardio.

chunks.title: Cardio while building muscle (interference effect)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: 2012 meta-analysis of mostly short studies; newer studies suggest interference may be smaller in well-fed, well-recovered trainees.

chunks.title: How muscles grow (mechanisms of hypertrophy)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Muscle grows when its fibers are exposed to enough mechanical tension, often enough, with enough food and recovery. Schoenfeld's 2010 review proposed three drivers: mechanical tension, metabolic stress (the "burn" and pump) and muscle damage. Since then, most researchers treat mechanical tension on working fibers as the main driver; stress and damage are side effects that may contribute a little at most.

chunks.title: How muscles grow (mechanisms of hypertrophy)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Tension on the muscle fibers, especially when sets get hard enough that most motor units are recruited, signals the muscle to add protein.
- Soreness and damage are not required for growth. Chasing soreness can cut into how much quality work you can do the following days.
- The pump is a sign of blood flow and metabolites, not proof a set was productive.

chunks.title: How muscles grow (mechanisms of hypertrophy)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Judge a session by hard sets close to failure with good technique and a full range of motion, not by soreness or pump.
- Progress the load or reps over weeks so the tension stays high as you get stronger.
- Recovery (sleep, protein, a calorie surplus when bulking) is where the growth is actually built.

chunks.title: How muscles grow (mechanisms of hypertrophy)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: This is a narrative review from 2010. Its three-mechanism model is a framework, not a proven formula, and the weight given to each mechanism has shifted with newer studies.

chunks.title: Strength training and injury prevention
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Strength training is one of the best-supported ways to prevent sports injuries. In a meta-analysis of randomized trials, strength training cut sports injuries to under a third, while static stretching showed no protective effect.

chunks.title: Strength training and injury prevention
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Warm up with lighter sets of the first lift instead of long static stretching.
- Progress loads gradually (small jumps, logged), keep 1-2 reps in reserve on heavy compound lifts, and use controlled technique.
- Train the back and rear delts at least as much as pressing to balance the shoulders.
- Sharp or worsening joint pain is a stop signal: swap the exercise and see a physio if it persists.

chunks.title: Strength training and injury prevention
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: The trials were in sports populations, not specifically bodybuilders, and injury definitions varied.

chunks.title: Heavy vs light weights and rep ranges
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Light, moderate and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure. Heavy loads build more maximal strength. So the rep range is mostly a practical choice: pick what lets you train hard, safely and consistently.

chunks.title: Heavy vs light weights and rep ranges
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Schoenfeld 2017: low-load (about 60% of 1RM or less) and high-load training produced similar hypertrophy when sets went to failure; high loads won for 1RM strength.
- Lopez 2021: across low, moderate and high loads, hypertrophy was similar; strength favored heavier loads.

chunks.title: Heavy vs light weights and rep ranges
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Use about 5-30 reps per set for growth. Most sets in the 6-15 range are efficient: heavy enough to progress, not so many reps that fatigue and discomfort end the set early.
- Keep heavier work (about 4-8 reps) on compound lifts if you also want strength.
- Very high-rep sets (20-30) are fine for joints-friendly isolation work but are uncomfortable and easy to stop short of failure.

chunks.title: Heavy vs light weights and rep ranges
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: "Close to failure" matters: light sets stopped far from failure grow less. Most studies are in untrained or recreationally trained people over short periods.

chunks.title: Training muscles at long lengths (stretch position)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Exercises that load a muscle while it is stretched tend to grow it more than versions that load it shortened. Two well-run trials show this: seated leg curls (hips bent, hamstrings long) beat lying leg curls, and overhead triceps extensions beat pushdowns for triceps growth.

chunks.title: Training muscles at long lengths (stretch position)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Maeo 2021: 12 weeks of seated leg curls produced clearly more hamstring growth than lying leg curls.
- Maeo 2023: overhead elbow extensions produced substantially more triceps growth than the same work with arms at the sides, including in the lateral and medial heads.

chunks.title: Training muscles at long lengths (stretch position)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Prefer stretch-loaded options: seated over lying leg curls, overhead extensions in addition to pushdowns, incline curls or preacher curls for biceps, deep-stretch flyes, deficit or full-depth calf raises, Romanian deadlifts.
- Use a full range of motion and control the stretched part of the rep instead of bouncing.

chunks.title: Training muscles at long lengths (stretch position)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Small samples of untrained or lightly trained adults. Not every muscle has been tested, and "lengthened partials" alone are still emerging evidence.

chunks.title: Progressive overload (adding weight or reps)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: To keep growing, the work has to get harder over time. Adding weight and adding reps at the same weight both work: in Plotkin 2022, progressing load or progressing reps produced similar muscle growth over 8 weeks, with small differences in strength measures.

chunks.title: Progressive overload (adding weight or reps)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Progressing reps (same weight, more reps) gave similar hypertrophy to progressing load.
- Progressing load was a little better for 1RM squat strength; rep progression was a little better for muscular endurance.

chunks.title: Progressive overload (adding weight or reps)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Use double progression: choose a rep range (for example 8-12). When you hit the top of the range on all sets with good form, add the smallest weight jump and start again at the bottom.
- Log every working set (the app does this) and aim to beat the last session by a rep or a small amount of weight.
- If a lift stalls for 3 sessions: check sleep and food first, then swap the variation or reduce fatigue, before adding more volume.

chunks.title: Progressive overload (adding weight or reps)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: One 8-week trial in trained-but-not-elite men. Long-term progress also depends on eating enough, sleep and exercise selection.

chunks.title: How close to failure to train (RIR)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sets need to be hard to grow muscle, but going all the way to failure on every set is not necessary. Growth tends to rise as sets get closer to failure, while strength gains are much less sensitive to it.

chunks.title: How close to failure to train (RIR)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Refalo 2023: training to failure and stopping short produced similar hypertrophy overall; the authors suggest stopping a few reps short is enough if sets are genuinely hard.
- Robinson 2024: hypertrophy increased as estimated reps in reserve went down (closer to failure); strength did not show the same relationship.

chunks.title: How close to failure to train (RIR)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Most working sets: 0-3 reps in reserve (you could do 0-3 more clean reps).
- Take the last set of isolation and machine exercises to failure; keep heavy barbell squats, deadlifts and bench a rep or two short for safety and recovery.
- Check yourself: if you often "had 5 more reps", the set was too easy to count as a hard set.

chunks.title: How close to failure to train (RIR)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: People are bad at guessing reps in reserve, especially on high-rep sets. Most data are short-term and in less-trained lifters.

chunks.title: Rest time between sets
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Short rest (about 1 minute) can reduce how much work you get done in later sets. In trained men, 3-minute rests produced more strength and more growth in some measures than 1-minute rests over 8 weeks.

chunks.title: Rest time between sets
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Rest about 2-3 minutes on heavy compound lifts, 1-2 minutes on isolation work.
- Rest until you can repeat a quality set, not by a strict clock. If reps crash on set two, rest longer.
- Short on time: use supersets of non-competing muscles (for example biceps with triceps) instead of cutting rest on big lifts.

chunks.title: Rest time between sets
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Single 8-week trial with a small sample. Volume was matched by sets, not by total work, which partly explains the result.

chunks.title: How often to train each muscle (frequency)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: When weekly sets are the same, training a muscle once, twice or three times a week grows it about equally. Frequency matters mainly as a tool to fit in enough quality volume: splitting 16 sets into two or three sessions keeps each set fresher than doing them all in one day.

chunks.title: How often to train each muscle (frequency)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- 2016 meta-analysis: training a muscle at least twice a week produced more growth than once, but many of those studies also differed in volume.
- 2019 meta-analysis, volume-equated: no meaningful difference in hypertrophy across frequencies.

chunks.title: How often to train each muscle (frequency)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Hit each muscle about twice a week as a default. Split very high weekly volume across more sessions.
- Pick the split you will actually follow. Push/pull/legs twice a week, upper/lower four days, or full body three days all work.
- For a lagging muscle, adding a third short session with a few hard sets is an easy way to add volume without long workouts.

chunks.title: How often to train each muscle (frequency)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Studies are mostly 6-12 weeks and in young adults. Very high frequencies (5-6 times a week per muscle) are less studied.

chunks.title: Building the upper chest (incline pressing)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The upper (clavicular) chest is best targeted with incline pressing. The one longitudinal trial comparing flat, incline and both found that only the incline group grew the upper chest clearly more. It is early evidence from untrained men, so treat it as a strong lean, not a law.

chunks.title: Building the upper chest (incline pressing)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Chaves 2020: 47 untrained men, 8 weeks, once a week. Incline-only pressing increased upper-chest thickness more than flat-only or a mix; other chest regions did not differ.
- EMG studies generally show more upper-chest activity on incline angles, but EMG does not reliably predict growth.

chunks.title: Building the upper chest (incline pressing)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Put an incline press (barbell, dumbbell, Smith or machine, roughly 30-45 degrees) first on at least one chest day, for 3-4 hard sets.
- Add low-to-high cable flyes or incline flyes for stretch under load.
- Keep total chest volume and progressive overload in place; angle choice only shifts where the growth goes.
- Check progress with photos from the same angle and light every 4-6 weeks.

chunks.title: Building the upper chest (incline pressing)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Single small longitudinal trial in untrained men training once a week; results in trained lifters may be smaller. Upper-chest shape is also influenced by genetics and body fat.

chunks.title: Building the upper chest (incline pressing)
chunks.heading: Conflicting evidence
chunks.text: Acute swelling data suggested flat bench may hit the upper chest similarly. Reviewers consider the longitudinal data more informative but still thin.

chunks.title: Weekly training volume (hard sets per muscle)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: More hard sets per muscle per week generally means more growth, up to a point. Schoenfeld's 2017 meta-analysis found a graded dose-response: about 10 or more weekly sets per muscle produced more growth than fewer. Newer analyses suggest the benefit keeps rising with volume but with diminishing returns, so each extra set buys less.

chunks.title: Weekly training volume (hard sets per muscle)
chunks.heading: Key findings
chunks.text:
- Schoenfeld 2017: each added weekly set was associated with a small extra increase in muscle size; 10+ sets a week beat fewer than 5.
- Baz-Valle 2022: roughly 12-20 weekly sets per muscle looked like a sensible range for trained people; going higher did not reliably add more.
- Pelland 2024 (preprint, not yet peer reviewed when checked): growth kept increasing with volume with clear diminishing returns, while strength gains plateaued sooner.

chunks.title: Weekly training volume (hard sets per muscle)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Count only hard sets (within about 0-3 reps of failure) for the muscle that is actually the main mover.
- Start a lagging muscle at about 10-12 hard sets a week and add 2-4 sets when progress stalls and recovery is good, rather than jumping to very high volume.
- If performance drops for 2+ weeks, joints ache, or sleep is poor, cut volume before adding more.
- For a bulk with limited time, put extra sets on the 1-3 muscles you most want to bring up, and keep the rest at maintenance-to-moderate volume.

chunks.title: Weekly training volume (hard sets per muscle)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Most studies last 6-12 weeks, use young men, and measure muscle thickness in one spot. Set counting rules differ (for example whether bench press counts for triceps). Individual response varies a lot.

chunks.title: Paying off debt: snowball vs avalanche
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Math says pay the highest interest rate first (avalanche). Behavior research says small wins keep people going: in data from about 6,000 debt-settlement clients, closing more individual accounts predicted finishing the program, even for the same dollars repaid. Lab work found people finish tasks faster when the parts go from smallest to largest.

chunks.title: Paying off debt: snowball vs avalanche
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- If rates are close, or motivation is the problem, pay minimums on all and attack the smallest balance first.
- If one debt has a much higher rate (for example a credit card at 25%+), attack that first.
- Never miss minimum payments; set autopay.

chunks.title: Paying off debt: snowball vs avalanche
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: The debt data came from people in a settlement program; dollar repayment and accounts closed were highly correlated. General education only.

chunks.title: Emergency fund first
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Even small amounts of easy-to-reach savings make a big difference in avoiding debt spirals. When the CFPB launched its savings initiative, it noted that 40% of Americans could not cover a $400 emergency from their own savings. A starter cushion comes before investing aggressively.

chunks.title: Emergency fund first
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Step 1: a starter fund of about one month of essentials in a separate high-yield savings account.
- Step 2: build toward 3-6 months of essentials; aim for the higher end with irregular self-employment income (videography).
- Automate a transfer on payday so saving happens before spending.
- Use the fund only for true emergencies and refill it first afterward.

chunks.title: Emergency fund first
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: This is general education, not personal financial advice. The 3-6 month range is a common planning convention, not a law.

chunks.title: Taxes on side business income (self-employment tax)
chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Profit from a side business like videography is subject to self-employment tax of 15.3% (12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare) on top of income tax. You must file Schedule SE when net self-employment earnings are $400 or more. The employer-equivalent part of SE tax is deductible when figuring adjusted gross income. Self-employed people may need to pay quarterly estimated taxes.

chunks.title: Taxes on side business income (self-employment tax)
chunks.heading: Practical application
chunks.text:
- Set aside a share of every client payment (many self-employed people use about 25-30%) in a separate tax savings account until you know your real rate.
- Track business expenses (camera gear, software, mileage) to reduce taxable profit.
- Check whether quarterly estimated payments apply (IRS Publication 505) once side income becomes regular.
- A tax professional is worth it the first year the business is meaningful.

chunks.title: Taxes on side business income (self-employment tax)
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: General education, not tax advice. Thresholds and rules change; re-verify each year.
